title: Half Symbol Bench
context: Grade 4. An adult sees half pictures and a sum. What is actually being learnt is that half a symbol stands for half of what the key says, and that adding a pictograph's rows answers how many in all only when nothing sits in two rows. The exercise this tool serves adds the interchange stations of five metro lines; an interchange station is where lines meet, so a station shared by two of those lines is in both rows, and the sum counts stations on lines, not separate stations. The chapter never shows a pictograph being totalled and never says how a half symbol is drawn.

writeup.why: Read what half a symbol stands for, read rows that end in a half, add the rows for a total, and see when a sum counts one thing more than once.
writeup.look: A bench with a key card that folds, a pictograph board in the middle, a total bar under it, and a small route map at one side.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only. 'Half Symbol Bench' sits in ink at the far left, with a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it. The phase title sits beside the dot on the same line, then the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart stand as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the whole symbols counted, and beside them a half once a half symbol has been counted, in ink, and under that the rows read against the rows on the board. The whole count climbs by one for each whole symbol, and the rows read climb by one as each row's sum lands. What the symbols stand for is never written here, and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The key card stands at the left of the working area, 220 by 200 at 64,212, with one whole symbol drawn 120 across and what it stands for written under it. The fold control sits under it, 220 by 56 at 64,424. It folds the symbol down its upright middle like paper, so the left half stands alone, and writes half the key beside it in amber. The fold is offered only when the key halves into whole things; on a key that does not, the control stays shut. The pair-up tray sits under the fold, 220 by 170 at 64,494. The board fills the middle, 560 by 440 at 300,212, with its title strip along its top, 560 by 44. Below it stand up to five row bands, each 72 tall, from 264 to 624. Each band has the row's name in a cell 110 wide at the left. Its symbols run from 420, each 40 wide with 8 between, up to seven whole symbols and one half. The half is the left half of the whole, 20 wide, and it comes last. The row's sum sits in a tag 70 wide at 786. The row reader writes the band's parts line under its symbols in amber: the whole symbols times the key, add half the key. The pair-up control slides two half symbols from different rows into the tray, where they click together into one whole symbol. The total bar lies under the board, 560 by 56 at 300,668, and adds every row once, writing the sum in reddish purple. It is labelled with what it counts: things in all when nothing sits in two rows, and things in rows when something does. The route map stands at the right, 270 by 512 at 876,212. It shows up to three routes, each a near-black line with its name at its end and its stops as amber dots 14 across. A stop that two routes share sits where their lines cross and is drawn in reddish purple. The share finder works on the map. A tap on a shared stop hangs a reddish purple tag with that stop's name beside every row that counts it. On a board whose key is one stop for each symbol, it rings the very symbol as well. Down the right of the canvas the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92), which holds what the child has given. That rectangle is the same on every phase and is never animated in or out. Under it is the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a number is asked for, with a key for a half beside them. On the fourth phase two keys stand under them, yes and no, and a word pad carries the words once, twice, three times, stops on routes and separate stops. The footer runs 758 to 900. The voice caption sits at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling. The phase bar sits at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, taken from its pictures. Every upright tally mark is deep blue, and every fifth mark, drawn across the four before it, is vermilion. Every pictograph symbol, whole or half, in the key and in the rows, is green, except where the rows are named by colour. There each row's symbols wear that row's own colour: red, green, blue, yellow or purple. The key's symbol there is plain grey, which stands for one symbol of any colour and is used for nothing else. Amber is what a row, a column or a tally stands for once it is read, and so are the numbers in a table and the numbers a side ruler writes. Amber too is what half a symbol stands for, what a key leaves over, and a small round counter for one thing counted. A total of every row is reddish purple, and so is a thing a total counts more than once, such as a stop two routes share. The row a question asks about is marked by a pale sky blue band laid behind its symbols, never over them. So is the stretch by which one row or tally reaches beyond another. Chrome never borrows one of those, and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every table rule, row line, belt, route line, bracket, outlined blank and card edge is near-black, and titles, row names, headings and the wording of every key are near-black type. Every reading survives with the colour taken away. A fifth mark lies across and not upright, and a half symbol is the left half of the whole. A row's number sits beyond its end, a total sits in its own bar or cell, and a band lies behind a row rather than on it. No amount is ever drawn as a length of colour: an amount on this stage is symbols, marks, counters or a written number. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box, never a faded copy of its answer. A half symbol is drawn nowhere but last in its row, and no part of a symbol other than a half is ever drawn. The total bar is never labelled as separate things while the share finder has a shared stop lit.
writeup.finish: The card shows the rows the child read, each with its whole part and its half written under it, the total they found, and the route map with the shared stop lit in both rows.

phases.win: the symbol folds, its left half stands alone, and half the key is written beside it
phases.does: folds the symbol down its middle and says what the half stands for
phases.goal: half a symbol stands for half of what the key says
phases.says: The whole one stands for this many. What does half of it stand for?
phases.check: One picture stands for eight pencils. What does half a picture stand for?
phases.feels: the symbol folds like paper, and its worth splits into two equal heaps along the same crease
phases.hands: Before the tool is opened, cut paper symbols in half with the class, straight down the middle, and keep the left half. With a key of two, four or ten, ask what the half stands for. Then try a key of three children, and let the class find that half of three is not a whole number of children. The chapter's two keys that use a half, four kites and two stations, both halve into whole things. It never says how a half is drawn, so draw the left half of the whole, as its own keys show it.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what does the whole symbol stand for? Second rung, the phase's: what is half of that? Third rung: the key is cut to a symbol for two, and the child folds it and says what the half holds. The number keys stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: a piece of a picture looks like one small thing, and one is the smallest number there is.
wrong.move: reads half a bottle picture as one bottle, as though any piece of a picture stood for one thing.
wrong.screen: the fold runs again, and the line of six counters under the symbol splits down the crease into two heaps of three. The half keeps its three, and the key card writes three beside it in amber. The child's one stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the half is the same picture, and a picture has stood for the whole key every time so far.
wrong.move: reads the half symbol as a whole one, six bottles, because it is the same picture.
wrong.screen: the whole symbol is drawn beside the half at the same height and twice as wide. The fold closes the whole down its crease onto the half, and the two edges meet. Three is written under the half, and six under the whole.

wrong.why: every key so far has folded, and the fold control looks as though it works on any key.
wrong.move: asks for a half symbol on a key of three children.
wrong.screen: the fold control stays shut. The key card lays its three counters under the symbol and draws the crease through the middle counter, which no fold can share between two halves. The key card stays as it was.

phases.screen: the key card with one whole symbol and what it stands for, and the fold waiting
phases.soWhat: Half a symbol stands for half of what the key says.

phases.win: the two parts are written under the row and their sum lands at its end
phases.does: reads the whole symbols with the key, then adds what the half stands for
phases.goal: a row ending in a half is its whole symbols times the key, add half the key
phases.says: Read the whole ones first. Then what does the half add?
phases.check: One picture stands for ten trees. How many trees do three and a half pictures show?
phases.feels: the whole symbols first, then the half, two parts written under the row and added
phases.hands: Hold up a row of paper symbols with a half at its end and a key of eight. Cover the half and read the whole symbols first, then uncover it and add half the key. The chapter's kites pictograph reads its yellow row this way: two whole kites at four and a half kite at two, ten kites. Ask what the row would show if the half were read as a whole, and why that would be wrong.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many whole symbols are there? Second rung, the phase's: what does the half add? Third rung: the row is cut to one whole symbol and a half, and the child reads each part. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: the half is the same picture as the others, and five pictures stand in the row.
wrong.move: counts the half as a whole symbol, and writes forty for four whole bus pictures and a half.
wrong.screen: the parts line writes the four whole symbols as thirty-two and the half as four, and the row's sum lands as thirty-six. The running count shows four and a half, never five. The child's forty stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the key card shows a whole symbol, and the half does not look like it.
wrong.move: leaves the half out and writes thirty-two, because only the whole symbols match the key card.
wrong.screen: the parts line writes thirty-two under the whole symbols, then lights the half and writes four under it. The two parts are added to thirty-six. The child's thirty-two stays beside it.

phases.screen: a pictograph row of whole symbols with a half symbol at its end, the key card beside it
phases.soWhat: A row ending in a half is its whole symbols times the key, add half the key.
phases.concept: A row that ends in a half

phases.win: the total fills the bar, and two halves slide together into one whole symbol
phases.does: adds every row into the total bar, then pairs two halves into one whole to check it
phases.goal: a pictograph's total is every row added once, when nothing sits in two rows
phases.says: Add every row. Does each thing sit in one row only?
phases.check: Rows stand for fourteen, nine and eleven apples, each apple in one basket. How many apples in all?
phases.feels: every row added once into the bar, and two halves from different rows making one whole
phases.hands: Put three rows of paper symbols on the board and ask how many things they show in all. The chapter asks for a total three times and never shows a pictograph being totalled; it is only adding. Before adding, ask whether any one thing could sit in two rows. Here each sapling was planted by one class, so none can.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does each row stand for? Second rung, the phase's: does any one thing sit in two rows? Third rung: the board is cut to two rows, and the child adds them into the bar. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: a half symbol is still a symbol, and whole symbols are what the key counts.
wrong.move: counts each half as a whole symbol, and writes sixty-four for rows of five and a half, three, and six and a half at four each.
wrong.screen: each row's parts line is written again: twenty and two, twelve, and twenty-four and two. The total bar adds the rows, twenty-two, twelve and twenty-six, and sixty lands. The two halves then pair up in the tray into one whole. The child's sixty-four stays in the slot.

wrong.why: adding the rows has been the whole job, and the symbols are what was counted.
wrong.move: adds the symbols and gives fifteen as the saplings, forgetting the key.
wrong.screen: the running count shows the fifteen symbols once the two halves have paired up. The total bar adds the rows' numbers, and sixty lands, labelled saplings in all. The child's fifteen stays beside the running count, where symbols are counted.

wrong.why: the halves look like leftovers, and leftovers are easy to leave out of a sum.
wrong.move: adds only the whole symbols and drops both halves, writing fifty-six.
wrong.screen: the pair-up control slides the two halves into the tray, where they click into one whole symbol, worth four. The total bar adds it to the fifty-six, and sixty lands. The child's fifty-six stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a pictograph of three rows, some ending in a half, with every row read and the total bar empty
phases.soWhat: A pictograph's total is every row added once, and it counts each thing once when nothing sits in two rows.
phases.concept: Adding the rows for a total

phases.win: the shared stop lights in both rows, and the total bar is relabelled as stops on routes
phases.does: taps the shared stop on the map and watches it light in each row that counts it
phases.goal: when one thing sits in two rows, adding the rows counts it twice
phases.says: Is this stop in one row, or in both? How many times does the sum count it?
phases.check: Two clubs of eight and six children share two children. What do the rows add up to, and is that the children?
phases.feels: the shared stop is tagged beside each row that counts it, and the sum is seen counting it twice
phases.hands: Draw two bus routes on the board that cross at one stop, and list the stops of each. Ask how many stops each route has, then add them, and ask whether the sum is the number of stops. The metro exercise adds the interchange stations of five lines. An interchange station is where lines meet, so a station shared by two of those lines sits in both rows. The rows' sum counts stations on lines, and the rows alone cannot say how many separate stations there are.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which stop is on both routes? Second rung, the phase's: how many rows count that stop? Third rung: the map is cut to two short routes of three stops each, sharing one, and the child taps the shared stop. The yes and no keys stay open.

wrong.why: adding the rows has given how many in all every time before.
wrong.move: gives eleven as the number of separate stops, when the stop the two routes share sits in both rows.
wrong.screen: the share finder lights the shared stop on the map, and a reddish purple tag with its name hangs beside both rows. The total bar is relabelled stops on routes. The child's eleven stays in the slot.

wrong.why: counting the stop once seems fair, and leaving it out of one row seems to mend the sum.
wrong.move: leaves the shared stop out of one route's row, so that the rows add up to separate stops.
wrong.screen: that route's line on the map is lit, and its stop dots are counted one at a time: five. Its row holds four, so the row no longer says how many stops the route has. The dot with no symbol is ringed, and the child's row stays as it was.

wrong.why: the shared stop has just been counted twice, and now every sum looks suspect.
wrong.move: will not add the rows of a pictograph whose rows share nothing, sure that any sum counts something twice.
wrong.screen: the saplings board has no route map, and the share finder finds nothing to light, because each sapling sits in one class's row only. The total bar adds the rows and keeps its label, saplings in all.

phases.screen: the route map with two routes crossing at one stop, and the pictograph of stops on each route
phases.soWhat: When one thing sits in two rows, adding the rows counts it twice. The rows alone cannot say how many separate things there are.

writeup.delight: The first phase, when the fold closes. Under the whole symbol the key's worth of small amber counters stands in a line. As the symbol folds, the line splits down the same crease into two equal heaps, one under each half. The left half keeps its heap, and the right half folds away with the other. It runs as often as a finger likes on any key that halves into whole things, nothing is marked either way, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the key card stands at the left holding one whole symbol and what it stands for, with the fold control waiting under it and the board empty. On the second one row stands on the board, whole symbols and a half at its end, with its parts line empty. On the third three rows stand, some ending in a half, each one read, with the total bar empty and the pair-up tray open. On the fourth the route map stands at the right with two routes crossing at one stop, and the board holds a row of stops for each route. The running count at the top left holds the whole symbols and halves counted, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the key's symbol, or the half at a row's end, or the total bar, or the stop where the routes cross, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks its question. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any key that halves into whole things, any rows of whole and half symbols, and any small map of routes, with the fold, the pair-up, the total bar and the share finder all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on what half a symbol stands for, rows that end in a half, totals of rows that share nothing, and sums that count a shared thing more than once.
voiceLines: One whole picture on the key card. What would half of it stand for?
The whole one stands for this many. What does half of it stand for?
Read the whole ones first. Then what does the half add?
Add every row. Does each thing sit in one row only?
Is this stop in one row, or in both? How many times does the sum count it?
Another row. Fold the key's symbol before you read the half.
Free play. Any key that halves into whole things, any rows, and any routes.
Read the whole symbols first, then the half, and put the two together.
Halves read from the key, rows added up, and a shared stop found in both rows.

observations.why: A half symbol stands for half of what one whole symbol stands for.
observations.soWhat: Half a symbol stands for half of what the key says, not for one thing.
observations.observe: The folded symbol stood as its left half, and half the key was written beside it.

observations.why: The whole symbols and the half stand for different amounts, so each part is read on its own first.
observations.soWhat: A row ending in a half is its whole symbols times the key, add half the key.
observations.observe: The parts line wrote what the whole symbols stand for and what the half stands for, and the row's sum was the two added.

observations.why: Two halves of the same symbol make one whole symbol's worth.
observations.soWhat: A pictograph's total adds every row once, and two halves in it make one whole. It counts each thing once when nothing sits in two rows.
observations.observe: Two halves from different rows clicked together into one whole in the tray, and the total did not change.

observations.why: Each route's row counts every stop on that route, the shared one too.
observations.soWhat: When one thing sits in two rows, adding the rows counts it twice, and the rows alone cannot say how many separate things there are.
observations.observe: The shared stop's tag hung beside both rows, and the total bar changed its label to stops on routes.

source_tool.description: A bench fills the stage with a key card at its left, a pictograph board in the middle and a small route map at its right. The key card holds one whole symbol, and a fold control folds it down its middle so its left half stands alone, and writes what the half stands for, half of the key, beside it; the fold is offered only for a key that halves into whole things. A row reader counts a row's whole symbols, takes the key that many times, and then adds half the key for a half symbol at the row's end, writing the two parts and their sum under the row. A pair-up control slides two half symbols from different rows together into one whole, so two halves are seen to make one symbol's worth. A total bar adds every row once and writes the sum under the board. A share finder works with the route map: the map shows each route's stops as dots on its own line, and a stop that two routes share sits where their lines cross. Tapping a shared stop lights it in every row that counts it, so the sum of the rows is seen to count it once for each route that uses it.
source_tool.art_direction: A folding key card beside a map / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a desk with a drawn class and a heap of answer slips, a ruled table, a tally board with a belt of answer cards, pictograph boards with a title strip and a key card, symbols that fold down their middle, a small route map, a tray of picture stamps, and a key dial.
Every pictograph carries a title strip at its top and a key card beside it from the first frame. A title or key still to be filled is an outlined blank, never a space left out.

Every symbol in one pictograph is one plain picture drawn at one size, evenly spaced from the same edge in every row or column, so a row's length is its count of symbols. A face, a kite, a cup, a tree or a bus; no letter, sign or mark ever stands in for a picture.

When the rows of a pictograph name colours, each row's symbols, whole or half, are drawn in that row's colour, and the key's symbol in plain grey. Otherwise every symbol in one pictograph, the key's included, is drawn in one colour.

A half symbol is the left half of the whole symbol, cut down its middle, as the chapter's own keys show it. It always comes last in its row. Halves are the only part of a symbol ever drawn, and only on a key that halves into whole things.
A tally mark is one short upright line. Every fifth mark is drawn across the four before it, corner to corner, and the next mark starts a new bundle after a small gap.
A pictograph drawn up the page stacks its symbols from the bottom. Its side is left unnumbered, or numbered only in the data's own units, the key times the symbols counted, and never in symbols.

The count of symbols and the number they stand for are never written in the same place: symbols are counted at the top left of the canvas, and a row's number is written at the end of its row with its unit.
The sum of every row is written under the board, labelled as the total for all the rows, and never beside a single row.
A row, a symbol or a mark is told apart by its name or its position first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a tally mark, a symbol, a number, a band or a slot the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. Every upright tally mark is deep blue, and the fifth mark, drawn across the four before it, is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter that counts in fives cannot afford a bundle whose closing mark has to be hunted for. Every pictograph symbol, whole or half, in the key and in every row, is green, except where the rows are told apart by colour: there every symbol in a row is that row's own colour, red, green, blue, yellow or purple, and the key's symbol is plain grey, a grey used for nothing else, because it stands for a symbol of any colour. What a row, a column or a tally stands for once it is read, the number written beyond a row's end, the numbers in a table, the numbers a side ruler writes in the data's own units, what half a symbol stands for, and what a key leaves over, is amber. A total of every row, and a thing that a total counts more than once, such as a stop two routes share, are reddish purple. The row a question asks about, and the stretch by which one row or tally reaches beyond another, are marked by a pale sky blue band behind the symbols or marks. Every table rule, row line, belt, bracket, outlined blank and card border is near-black chrome, and titles, row names, headings and the wording of every key are near-black type. All of that holds in greyscale, because a fifth mark lies across and not upright, a half symbol is the left half of the whole, a row's number sits beyond its end, a total sits in its own bar or cell, and a band lies behind a row rather than on it.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Read the whole symbols first, then the half, and put the two together.
voice.onNext: Another row. Fold the key's symbol before you read the half.
voice.opening: One whole picture on the key card. What would half of it stand for?
voice.onFinish: Halves read from the key, rows added up, and a shared stop found in both rows.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any key that halves into whole things, any rows, and any routes.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A row that ends in a half
Adding the rows for a total

placement.where: After groups have shown an odd count with paper symbols, a key of two and one symbol cut in half, and before the printed metro pictograph is read. The tool is what folds a symbol to show what its half stands for, and what lights a shared stop in every row that counts it, so a sum that counts one thing twice is seen doing it.

answer_key.rule: Half a symbol stands for half of what the key says, so a half symbol is used only with a key that halves into whole things. A row that ends in a half is its whole symbols times the key, add half the key, and two half symbols together stand for one whole symbol's worth. The total a pictograph shows is found by adding every row, and it counts each thing once only when nothing sits in two rows. When one thing sits in several rows, adding the rows counts it once for every row it is in, so the sum counts things in rows, not separate things.
answer_key.wrong: The row reader splits the row again into its whole symbols and its half, writing each part under the row, and the share finder relights the shared thing in every row it sits in. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Half a symbol stands for half of what the key says.
The key says 6, and 6 is 3 and 3.
So half a bottle picture stands for 3 bottles.
items.question: One bottle picture stands for 6 bottles. What does half a bottle picture stand for?
items.checkpoint: Half a symbol stands for half of what the key says.
items.misconception: Reading half a picture as 1 bottle, as though any piece of a picture stood for one thing.

steps: The 4 whole pictures stand for 4 x 8 = 32 children.
The half picture stands for half of 8, which is 4.
items.question: One bus picture stands for 8 children. A row holds 4 whole bus pictures and a half. How many children does it show?
items.checkpoint: A row ending in a half is its whole symbols times the key, add half the key.
items.misconception: Counting the half picture as a whole one and writing 40, or leaving it out and writing 32.

steps: Turn each row into a number. 5 and a half pictures is 20 + 2 = 22, 3 pictures is 12, and 6 and a half is 24 + 2 = 26.
Each sapling sits in one row only, so adding the rows counts each one once.
22 + 12 + 26 = 60 saplings. The two halves also pair up into one whole: 15 pictures, and 15 x 4 = 60.
items.question: A pictograph of saplings planted by three classes has the key one sapling picture for 4 saplings. The rows hold 5 and a half, 3, and 6 and a half pictures. Each sapling was planted by one class. How many saplings were planted in all?
items.checkpoint: Add every row for the total, when nothing sits in two rows.
items.misconception: Counting each half picture as a whole one and writing 64.

steps: Each route's row counts every stop on that route, the shared stop too.
Adding the rows counts the shared stop once for each route that uses it, so it is counted twice.
So 11 counts stops on routes, and there are fewer than 11 separate stops.
items.answer: No. The shared stop is in both rows, so 11 counts it twice. 11 counts stops on routes, not separate stops
items.question: Two bus routes, the hill route and the lake route, share one stop. A pictograph shows 6 stops for the hill route and 5 for the lake route, and each row counts the shared stop. The rows add up to 11. Is 11 the number of separate stops?
items.checkpoint: Adding the rows counts a shared thing once for every row it is in.
items.misconception: Giving 11 as the number of separate stops, when the stop the two routes share is counted twice.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: One tree picture stands for 10 trees. What does half a tree picture stand for?
A key says half a star stands for 4 stickers. What does a whole star stand for?
One book picture stands for 2 books. A row holds 5 whole book pictures and a half. How many books does it show?
items.final_answer: 11 books: 10 from the whole pictures and 1 from the half

items.question: One flag picture stands for 6 flags. Three rows hold 3 and a half, 5, and 2 and a half flag pictures. How many flags does each row show?
Rows stand for 18, 25 and 11 marbles, and each marble is in one bag only. How many marbles are there in all?
One jar picture stands for 10 jars of pickle. A shop's rows for three weeks hold 4, 2 and a half, and 3 and a half jar pictures. How many jars were sold in the three weeks?
Three clubs list their members: art 9, music 7 and chess 6. Two children are in both art and music. The rows add up to 22. Is 22 the number of separate children in the clubs?
items.final_answer: No. Each child in both art and music is counted twice, once in each row, so 22 counts each child once for every club they are in

items.question: A pictograph shows the stops of three bus routes, one stop picture for 2 stops. The rows hold 3 pictures, 2 and a half pictures, and 4 pictures. All three routes stop at the market. What do the rows add up to, and how many times is the market stop counted in that sum?
items.final_answer: 19, because 6 + 5 + 8 = 19. The market stop is counted three times, once in each row

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: shows one whole symbol and what it stands for
folds the key's symbol down its middle and writes what the half stands for
reads the whole symbols and a half at the end, writing both parts and their sum
slides two half symbols together into one whole
adds every row once and writes the sum under the board
shows each route's stops as dots on its own line
lights a shared stop in every row that counts it

teaching_notes: Cut paper symbols in half before the tool is opened, and let groups show an odd count, such as the pencils in a tin, with a key of two and one half symbol at a row's end. The chapter never says how a half symbol is drawn: draw the left half of the whole symbol, cut down its middle, as the chapter's own keys show it, and put it last in its row. Use a half symbol only with a key that halves into whole things, such as two, four or ten, because half of a key of three is not a whole number of anything. The chapter asks for a total three times and never shows a pictograph being totalled; it is only adding. The exercise this tool serves adds the interchange stations of five metro lines. An interchange station is where lines meet, so a station shared by two of those lines sits in both rows, and adding the rows counts it twice. Say that the sum counts stations on lines, not separate stations, and that the pictograph cannot say how many separate stations there are. Draw two routes crossing at one stop on the board and let the class find that stop in both rows.
generation_prompt: Build a half symbol tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A key card at the left of the working area shows one whole symbol and what it stands for; a fold control folds the symbol down its upright middle so its left half stands alone, and writes half the key beside it, and the fold is offered only when the key halves into a whole number. A pictograph board in the middle holds up to five rows of one symbol at one size, evenly spaced from the same left edge, with at most one half symbol, the left half of the whole, at the end of a row. A row reader writes under any row its whole symbols times the key, half the key for a half symbol, and their sum at the row's end. A pair-up control slides two half symbols from different rows together into one whole. A total bar under the board adds every row once. A small route map at the right shows up to three routes as lines of stop dots; a stop on two routes sits where their lines cross, and tapping it lights that stop's place in every row that counts it, with the total bar relabelled as stops on routes. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Fold the symbol to see what half of it stands for. Read the whole symbols first. Then add the half. Add every row for the total. Tap a shared stop to see every row that counts it.
